## The Stationary Gravitational Field

The previous section prepared the source layer. This section gives the stationary field map that follows from it.

The central result is a direct map from the even source package to scalar gravitational depth. M1 treats momentum as the primary physical content, so the first field question is not how to rename a classical density or metric component. It is whether momentum content has a clean field response. In the stationary scalar sector, it does. The odd source also admits a useful transverse response seed, but that map remains a separate field-side assumption rather than the second projection of one primitive response law.

### Stationary source-to-field map

For each direction $k$, write the primitive momentum-density source channels as

$$
\mathcal{J}_k^+(x),
\qquad
\mathcal{J}_k^-(x).
$$

Here $x$ marks the source location at which the channel density is defined. In the integral formulas below, the source point is written as $r'$ and the observation point as $r$. The units of $\mathcal{J}_k^\pm$ are kg/(s m$^2$): momentum content per unit volume, sorted by directional sense, as fixed by the carrier map of the previous section.

Let

$$
R:=\|r-r'\|,
$$

where $r'$ is the source point and $r$ is the observation point, and let $e_{(k)}^i(r')$ be the local orthonormal basis vector associated with the direction label $k\in\{x,y,z\}$ at the source point. The stationary coupling is

$$
\kappa:=\frac{G_N}{c^3}.
$$

The source packages prepared in the previous section are

$$
\mathcal M_k
=
\frac{\mathcal J_k^++\mathcal J_k^-}{2},
\qquad
\mathcal P_k
=
\mathcal J_k^+-\mathcal J_k^-.
$$

SI makes the even package axis-independent:

$$
\mathcal M_k(r')=\mathcal M(r')
\qquad\text{for every }k.
$$

The stationary scalar field is therefore

$$
\boxed{
\theta_0(r)
=
\kappa\int_\Sigma
\frac{\mathcal M(r')}{\|r-r'\|}\,d^3r'}.
$$

There is one scalar source field and no axis sum to perform. Written directly in the primitive channels, any fixed $k$ gives

$$
\theta_0(r)
=
\frac{G_N}{2c^3}
\int_\Sigma
\frac{\mathcal J_k^+(r')+\mathcal J_k^-(r')}{\|r-r'\|}\,d^3r'.
$$

This is the achieved stationary source-to-field map.

The odd package motivates a separate transverse response seed,

$$
\theta_i^\perp(r)
=
\kappa\int_\Sigma
\frac{\mathcal P_i^\perp(r')}{\|r-r'\|}\,d^3r'.
$$

Written directly in the channel differences,

$$
\theta_i^\perp(r)
=
\frac{G_N}{c^3}
\left[
\sum_k\int_\Sigma
\frac{\mathcal J_k^+(r')-\mathcal J_k^-(r')}{\|r-r'\|}
e_{(k)i}(r')\,d^3r'
\right]^\perp .
$$

The basis vector $e_{(k)i}$ carries the source-axis label into the field component. The final transverse projection selects the stationary-admissible part of the odd source.

The scalar and directional maps share the economical $1/R$ kernel, but they have not been derived as two projections of one elementary directional field action. The scalar map is the achieved stationary backbone. The directional map is retained as a separate response assumption whose action and physical readout remain open. Independent $\mathcal C_{ij}$ contributions are neglected in this minimal map.

The supporting derivation and convention sheet are collected in [Appendix 3.4A](#sec-derivation-03-04A-source-field-map).

### Packaged field variables

The scalar well is packaged into the local gravitational clock factor

$$
G(r):=\sqrt{1-2\theta_0(r)}.
$$

Substituting the field map gives

$$
G(r)
=
\sqrt{
1-
\frac{G_N}{c^3}\int_\Sigma
\frac{\mathcal J_k^+(r')+\mathcal J_k^-(r')}{\|r-r'\|}\,d^3r'
}.
$$

This is the direct stationary expression for the clock-depth package in terms of $\mathcal J_k^\pm$, valid for any fixed axis $k$. The square root is an exact definition of the selected package. It does not turn the linear Green kernel into a nonlinear spatial field theory.

For later directional bookkeeping, the chapter reserves the observer-facing package

$$
A_i(r):=-\kappa_A\theta_i^\perp(r).
$$

Here $\kappa_A$ belongs to the packaging step, not to the source grammar. Its physical normalization and sign-bearing observer map are left to the stationary correspondence discussion. Written out,

$$
A_i(r)
=
-\kappa_A\frac{G_N}{c^3}
\int_\Sigma
\frac{\mathcal P_i^\perp(r')}{\|r-r'\|}\,d^3r'.
$$

The shift package also has circulation-like content,

$$
B_{ij}=D_iA_j-D_jA_i,
$$

where $D_i$ is the spatial covariant derivative. In a flat exterior chart this reduces to

$$
B_{ij}=\partial_iA_j-\partial_jA_i.
$$

The scalar package $G$ carries the achieved clock-depth result. The quantities $A_i$ and $B_{ij}$ reserve notation for the provisional directional route used later in the chapter.

### The spatial-response boundary

The scalar well fixes the stationary clock-depth package, but it does not by itself fix a physical ruler. Earlier versions of the chapter treated spatial stretch as a second face of the same deformation. The carrier analysis places a sharper boundary: clock, ruler, and null motion must be read from one consistent generator.

The next section develops that carrier map and states the resulting reciprocal boundary. What is already secure here is the scalar Poisson construction. A physical spatial response remains a separate completion problem.

### Differential form

The integral map is the clearest statement. In a flat stationary exterior, the same map may be written as Poisson-type equations. Since

$$
\Delta\left(\frac{1}{R}\right)
=
-4\pi\delta^{(3)}(r-r'),
$$

the scalar equation is

$$
\boxed{
\Delta\theta_0(r)
=
-\frac{4\pi G_N}{c^3}\mathcal M(r)}.
$$

Equivalently, for any fixed $k$,

$$
\Delta\theta_0(r)
=
-\frac{2\pi G_N}{c^3}
\left(\mathcal J_k^+(r)+\mathcal J_k^-(r)\right).
$$

The provisional directional equation is

$$
\Delta\theta_i^\perp(r)
=
-\frac{4\pi G_N}{c^3}\mathcal P_i^\perp(r),
\qquad
\partial_i\theta_i^\perp=0.
$$

In channel form,

$$
\Delta\theta_i^\perp(r)
=
-\frac{4\pi G_N}{c^3}
\left[
\sum_k
\left(\mathcal J_k^+(r)-\mathcal J_k^-(r)\right)e_{(k)i}(r)
\right]^\perp .
$$

These equations display the source split at field level without treating the scalar and directional sectors as projections of one primitive response law.

### What the map says physically

The map makes the source grammar visible at the field level.

If the two directional senses of a source channel are balanced, their odd package cancels while their additive content remains. Such a source contributes to the scalar well but not to the directional seed along that channel.

If the two directional senses are imbalanced, the odd package survives. An organized flow or rotating distribution can therefore seed a transverse response in addition to the scalar well. The scalar well is present in both static and rotating sources; the odd package distinguishes the rotating one.

A single positive channel contributes to both the even source package and the odd imbalance. This fact belongs to the source algebra. It does not require the scalar and directional fields to share one microscopic response law.

### What the stationary field establishes

The stationary field construction establishes the route

$$
\mathcal M
\longrightarrow
\theta_0
\longrightarrow
G.
$$

The source is axis-independent under SI, the field follows the stationary $1/R$ kernel, and the same map has the Poisson form displayed above.

The directional route is narrower:

$$
\mathcal P_i^\perp
\longrightarrow
\theta_i^\perp
\longrightarrow
A_i.
$$

The first arrow is a provisional transverse response assumption; the second reserves observer-facing packaging for later correspondence. Neither changes the exact source identity $\mathcal P_i=j_i$.

The next section asks how particles, clocks, rulers, and local motion read the stationary scalar field, and where the directional diagnostics remain provisional.
